keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (Cliopatria has no row). Apulia, Calabria and Basilicata are the page's core regions; the page names no Salento or Theme of Calabria and gives no area. 'By 1040' the page says the Byzantines had lost most of Apulia, while the Norman conquest page has the battles of 1041; the shape runs to 1040. (Reviewer eu-05-x, 2026-10-19: 'to' 1040 -> 1042: no shape covered 1041-1042; the 1041 battles are contest only and William became Count of Apulia at Melfi in September 1042 (Norman conquest of southern Italy page), which ledger /ledger/2 dates as the loss)

The pages do not say which Basilicata towns stayed Byzantine (Matera is not on the pages), so all of Basilicata is dropped.

region.text: Apulia, Calabria and Basilicata, 'would remain firmly under Byzantine control until the 11th century' (the page's core regions)

ledger.note: About 965: Byzantine Italy gets a catepan. 'In c. 965, a new theme of Lucania was established' and the strategos of Bari was raised to katepano of Italy; the first listed katepano, Michael Abidelas, serves 970-975. Bari had 'passed under Byzantine control in 876', Otranto was taken from the Saracens in 873, and Nikephoros Phokas the Elder's expeditions of the mid-880s extended control over most of Apulia and Calabria.

region.text: Olivento near Venosa, Montemaggiore near Cannae and Montepeloso, where the Normans beat the catepans in 1041

ledger.note: 1041: the Normans defeat the Byzantines three times. 16 March 1041 at Olivento near Venosa; 4 May 1041 under William Iron Arm at Montemaggiore near Cannae ('Many Byzantine soldiers drowned in the Ofanto'); 3 September 1041 at Montepeloso, where the catepan Exaugustus Boioannes was taken to Benevento.

region.text: the north of the catepanate: Basilicata, Foggia and Barletta-Andria-Trani, held by the Normans of the new county of Apulia

ledger.note: September 1042: William Iron Arm becomes Count of Apulia. At the Melfi council 'William was made Count of Apulia by Guaimar'; the Catepanate page says the Byzantines had lost most of Apulia 'by 1040'. The pages give no Byzantine loss at Melfi; the land is the researcher's reading of where the 1041 battles were won.

September 1042: the Norman county of Apulia is organised at Melfi (Guaimar of Salerno's council). Byzantine counterstrokes follow: 'Argyrus defeated William near Taranto' in 1045 and 'Drogo defeated the catepan Eustathios Palatinos near Taranto' in 1046 (the page's words, as summarised), without recovering the north.

1060: Robert Guiscard takes Reggio. 'Robert Guiscard captured Reggio Calabria, the capital of the Calabrian tagma' in 1060. The page is silent on Squillace and Gerace and on 1057-59, so the rest of Calabria is the researcher's reading.

region.text: Apulia south of the Ofanto: the provinces of Bari, Taranto, Brindisi and Lecce (Salento)

ledger.note: 5 August 1068: the Normans besiege Bari. Robert Guiscard's forces began the siege; the pro-Byzantine faction prevailed and the barons sent envoys to Romanos IV for aid. Otranto, besieged by Count Geoffrey of Conversano, 'fell in October' (the page does not state the year but places it shortly after the 1068 siege began).
Autumn 1070: Brindisi capitulates. Robert moved there in January 1070 to help the siege; it 'capitulated in autumn 1070'.

region.text: Apulia south of the Ofanto: the provinces of Bari, Taranto, Brindisi and Lecce (Salento)

ledger.note: 16 April 1071: Bari falls. 'Bari was captured on 16 April 1071 when Robert Guiscard entered the city' (the infobox gives 15 April); the fall 'ended 536 years of Byzantine presence in southern Italy'. The page is silent on Taranto and Oria, which are folded into this loss.

region.text: Apulia south of the Ofanto: the provinces of Bari, Taranto, Brindisi and Lecce (Salento)

ledger.note: April 1071: the siege ends with Bari's surrender; the catepan Stephen Pateran was imprisoned and later allowed to return to Constantinople.

region.text: Apulia south of the Ofanto: the provinces of Bari, Taranto, Brindisi and Lecce (Salento)

ledger.note: April 1071: the Catepanate of Italy ends. 'Bari was captured by the Normans in April 1071' and 'Byzantine authority was finally terminated in Italy'. Manuel I Komnenos's reconquest attempt of 1156-58 failed (Siege of Bari page).

wars.name: Norman conquest of Byzantine Apulia
wars.outcome: The Normans beat the Byzantines at Olivento, Montemaggiore and Montepeloso in 1041; William Iron Arm was made Count of Apulia in September 1042; Argyrus beat William near Taranto (1045) and Drogo beat the catepan Eustathios near Taranto (1046).
wars.note: The Catepanate page says most of Apulia was lost 'by 1040'. The page is silent on the Melus and Arduin revolts of 1009-1018, the battle of Cannae (1018) and Troia (1018).

wars.name: Norman conquest of Calabria
wars.outcome: Robert Guiscard took Reggio Calabria, the capital of the Calabrian tagma, in 1060.
wars.note: The page is silent on 1057-59 and on Squillace and Gerace.

wars.name: Siege of Bari

zones.text: Apulia south of the Ofanto: the provinces of Bari, Taranto, Brindisi and Lecce (Salento)

wars.outcome: Bari was besieged from 5 August 1068 and captured on 16 April 1071; Otranto fell in October (1068 on the Norman-conquest page's account) and Brindisi in autumn 1070; Byzantine rule in southern Italy ended.
wars.note: The Catepanate and Norman conquest pages give April 1071 and no day.

certainty.note: The catepanate's frontier with the Lombard principalities of Benevento, Capua and Salerno and the Norman county is approximate; the pages name cities and battles, not lines.

notes: Written by eu-05-x (additions). Cliopatria has no row; slug free. Three pages opened; the Theme of Longobardia article did not load (404), so the 876-965 themes and the 891/892 foundation of Longobardia are not carried as a separate state; the Catepanate infobox dates the state from 965. Not settled: (1) no area on any page; (2) Taranto, Oria, Otranto's year and the rest of Calabria after 1060 are page-silent; (3) Basilicata towns that stayed Byzantine after 1042 (Matera) are not on the pages; (4) Byzantine Sicily (lost 827-902) and the Lombard principalities are other groups'; (5) the 1018 Cannae battle and the Melus revolt are page-silent.
